newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin lays down law on binding NATO treaty.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin lays down law on binding NATO treaty.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin laid out demanding terms on Sunday for any compromise on NATO's planned expansion, saying he would insist on a legally binding treaty barring Western forces from ever deploying in eastern Europe.

In an interview with a Finnish newspaper ahead of this week's Helsinki summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton, Yeltsin restated Moscow's strong objections to NATO enlargement, calling it a breach of promises made in 1990 at the end of the Cold War.

But, according to a text of the interview with Helsingin Sanomat published by Itar-Tass news agency, he said Russia could not veto the move and held out the prospect of reaching a an accord with NATO by this summer. Such a deal, he said, ought to lay the ground for a new conventional arms control treaty.

Yeltsin's comments, before a March 19-20 summit he has said will be his toughest ever, held out a mixture of hope -- on the timetable -- and a warning -- that Moscow intends to drive a hard bargain, notably by demanding that a new arms and security mechanism for Europe be legally binding, against NATO's wishes.

It would be "advisable", he said, to lay down the basis for a revised treaty on Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) in the NATO-Russia document -- "in any event by this summer". "We would consider this as an indicator of the alliance's declared readiness to take into account Russia's concerns," he said.

But he also stressed: "A document on the parameters of Russia-NATO relations should be binding. We intend to put it to ratification, because we cannot, on past experience, be satisfied with non-binding assurances."

NATO is anxious to complete a charter with Russia, defining their relations and giving Moscow a say in some NATO decisions, before its Madrid summit in July, where the western defence pact aims to invite former Soviet-bloc countries in eastern Europe to join -- most likely Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
At the same time, however, western countries have been resisting the idea of a full-blown treaty with Russia that would require complex ratification by national parliaments.
They have, instead, offered a series of undertakings, the latest of which was a renewed pledge on Friday not to station any permanent new troops in Europe for the foreseeable future.
Yeltsin's spokesman floated the idea last week that "ratification" of a binding treaty might not need parliamentary review, but Russia's final attitude to this remains unclear.
Yeltsin said he noted NATO's assurances that, for instance, it would not deploy nuclear weapons in new member states but insisted Russia wanted official, binding commitments.

He reserved the bulk of his comments to conventional forces, indicating that Russia saw revisions to the CFE treaty as a way of ensuring that NATO enlargement did not mean troops from the 16 present members coming closer to Russia's borders.
"A legally binding document should contain precisely formulated guarantees of Russia's security interests," he said.

"In the first instance, that NATO's military infrastructure will not advance to the East and that foreign troops and conventional weapons will not be moved beyond those territories where they are currently deployed."

Western diplomats say Russia, whose foreign minister, Yevgeny Primakov was in Washington at the weekend to prepare for the summit, is trying to extract the highest price for its acquiescent in the virtual fait accompli of NATO expansion.
Yeltsin, however, insisted that a NATO-Russia deal was not a "payoff" for Russia's blessing on NATO enlargement.
Maintaining his hostility to the pact's expansion, Yeltsin said: "It may lead to a slide toward new confrontation, to an undermining of trust between Russia and the western countries."
And he praised summit host Finland for not staying out of NATO. "It seems to us a worthy example for other countries which are now falling over themselves to join NATO," he said.
Primakov met U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Saturday. No details were released. He meets Defence Secretary William Cohen on Sunday and is due to see Clinton on Monday.
